title: Refresh before the first send
dek: Moving the expiry check ahead of dispatch lets the request wait for credential refresh before it leaves the client.
footer: PR #42 · fix: refresh credentials before dispatch

sections.title: A refresh that came after dispatch
sections.content:
The request function in client.ts already knew how to check credential expiry and refresh credentials. Before this change, it sent the payload first, checked the expiry time afterward, and then returned the response. Credential maintenance existed, but its position could not protect the request that had just been sent.

The author reports that the first request after expiry failed because of this ordering. The change addresses that specific sequence inside the ordinary request function. We can understand the fix by following when the client sends the payload, rather than by looking for a new refresh mechanism.

sections.title: The expired request went first
sections.content:
Imagine you call the function just after the credentials expire. In the old order, the client attempts the send before it asks whether those credentials are still current. A later refresh cannot change the credentials used by that earlier attempt. The author identifies the resulting cost as an initial failed request.

The expiry comparison treats a timestamp equal to the current time as expired, too. That boundary stays the same. What changes is whether the function makes the decision before or after dispatch: the check must happen early enough to affect the request it is meant to protect.

sections.title: Make refresh a prerequisite for sending
sections.content:
The function now starts with the existing expiry check. When the credentials have expired, await makes the function wait for refresh to complete before execution continues:

{{CODE:0}}

The important detail is the combination of placement and waiting. The check precedes dispatch, and refresh is awaited. When the comparison is false, execution proceeds directly to the send.

The remaining lines still send the supplied payload and return the resulting response:

{{CODE:1}}

This keeps the change local to ordering. The sole modified file is client.ts; its request function makes credential refresh a prerequisite when needed, while preserving the send-and-return sequence.

code.source:
const response = await client.send(payload);
return response;

sections.title: Pay the refresh cost before dispatch
sections.content:
Waiting protects the first attempt

An expired request now waits for refresh before sending. That ordering serves the author's stated goal: avoid the initial failed request. The PR body describes an extra clock read as an accepted cost, but the diff moves the existing Date.now() check. It does not show a second clock read being added.

The fix follows this function's boundary

The author says streaming requests use a separate path and still need a follow-up. That separate path explains why moving this check does not establish the same ordering for streaming. The supplied change covers the request function shown here.

sections.title: Carry the ordering fix to streaming
sections.content: Streaming is the documented follow-up. The next change needs to address credential timing on that separate path; this diff provides no streaming implementation to walk through. The materials supply neither a follow-up issue number nor a priority, so they establish the remaining scope without establishing a delivery plan.

sections.title: Check, refresh if needed, then send
sections.content: PR #42 moves the existing credential-expiry check ahead of dispatch and awaits refresh when needed. It addresses the reported first-request failure by changing when refresh happens, while retaining the response-returning sequence. The diff shows a moved clock check, not an added one. Streaming remains the explicit follow-up because it uses a separate request path.
